```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>",
                      fig.width = 6.5, fig.height = 4.5)
```

`qqrtools` estimates quantile-on-quantile regression (QQR) surfaces
\(\beta(\theta, \tau)\): the effect of the \(\theta\)-quantile of a regressor
\(X\) on the \(\tau\)-quantile of an outcome \(Y\) (Sim and Zhou, 2015).
This vignette runs a complete analysis on simulated data in which the true
surface is known. The methodology is explained in
`vignette("qqr-methodology")`.

## Simulated data with a known surface

Let \(X \sim U(0, 1)\), a control \(W \sim N(0, 1)\) and

\[
Y = 1 + 2X + 0.5W + (0.5 + X)\,\varepsilon, \qquad \varepsilon \sim N(0,1).
\]

The conditional \(\tau\)-quantile is
\(Q_Y(\tau \mid x, w) = 1 + 0.5\,\Phi^{-1}(\tau) + \{2 + \Phi^{-1}(\tau)\}x + 0.5w\),
so the true QQR slope is \(\beta(\theta, \tau) = 2 + \Phi^{-1}(\tau)\) for
every \(\theta\): the effect of \(X\) is larger in the upper tail of \(Y\),
and it does not depend on the quantile of \(X\).

```{r data}
library(qqrtools)
set.seed(2026)
n   <- 1000
dat <- data.frame(x = runif(n), w = rnorm(n))
dat$y <- 1 + 2 * dat$x + 0.5 * dat$w + (0.5 + dat$x) * rnorm(n)
```

## Fitting the model

```{r fit}
taus <- c(0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 0.9)
fit  <- qqr(y ~ x + w, data = dat, qvar = "x",
            taus = taus, thetas = c(0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 0.9))
fit
```

The grid points are the empirical \(\theta\)-quantiles of `x`:

```{r grid}
rbind(theta = fit$thetas, x = round(fit$grid, 3))
```

## The estimated surface

Rows are \(\theta\) (quantiles of `x`), columns are \(\tau\) (quantiles of
`y`):

```{r surface}
round(fit$qcoef, 2)
## true surface: the same value in every row
round(2 + qnorm(taus), 2)
```

The estimates reproduce the pattern of the true surface: slopes increase
with \(\tau\) and are similar across \(\theta\). Individual cells are
noisy, because each local regression uses only the observations near one
grid point. The noise depends strongly on the bandwidth:

```{r bandwidth}
err <- sapply(c(0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3), function(h) {
  f <- suppressWarnings(
    qqr(y ~ x + w, data = dat, qvar = "x", taus = taus,
        thetas = fit$thetas, h = h, se_type = "none"))
  sqrt(mean(sweep(f$qcoef, 2, 2 + qnorm(taus))^2))
})
data.frame(h = c(0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3), rmse = round(err, 3))
```

Because this DGP has a slope that is constant in \(\theta\), wider
bandwidths are always better here. When the true surface varies with
\(\theta\), a wide bandwidth smooths that variation away (bias).

The default rule, `h = "slope"`, uses the \(n^{-1/7}\) rate that is optimal
for local slopes, which is wider than density rules such as Silverman's,
and the default local quadratic fit (`degree = 2`) limits the bias at the
low and high quantiles of `x`. The rule used is stored in the fit:

```{r details}
cat(fit$h_details)
```

There is no universally right \(h\). `qqr_sensitivity()` refits the
surface for several multiples of the selected bandwidth and reports how
much it changes:

```{r sensitivity}
sens <- qqr_sensitivity(fit)
sens
plot(sens)
```

Interpret the features that are stable across bandwidths.

## Comparison with standard quantile regression

Averaging the surface over \(\theta\) should give roughly the standard QR
slope when the QR model is correctly specified (here it is):

```{r compare}
compare.qqr(fit, digits = 3)
```

## P-values

`fit$pval_surfaces` holds pointwise p-values from
`quantreg::summary.rq()` for every cell. They are descriptive: they ignore
the smoothing bias and the fact that many cells are examined. The default
`se_type = "ker"` is fast and slightly conservative; for results you
report, `se_type = "boot"` (after `set.seed()`) is closer to the nominal
level.

```{r pvalues}
round(fit$pval_surfaces$x, 3)
```

With many cells, some are significant by chance. `qqr_padjust()` adjusts
each surface for the number of cells (Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery
rate by default):

```{r padjust}
fit_adj <- qqr_padjust(fit)
round(fit_adj$pval_surfaces$x, 3)
```

## Graphics

```{r plot3d}
surface3d(fit, palette = "Blue-Red 3", add_zero_plane = FALSE, theta = 35)
```

```{r panels, fig.height = 3.5}
panel_surface(fit, coef = c("x", "w"))
```

Interactive versions are available with `qqr_heatmap()`, `qqr_contour()`
and `qqr_plotly()` (package *plotly*) and `Int.plot()` (package *rgl*).

## Tables and export

```{r tables}
head(qqr_surface(fit, coef = "x", digits = 3))
head(qqr_surface(fit, coef = c("x", "w"), long = TRUE, digits = 3))
```

`excel.qqr()`, `word.qqr()`, `excel.compare.qqr()` and
`word.compare.qqr()` write the same tables to *Excel* and *Word* files.

## Sim-Zhou weighting

Sim and Zhou (2015) use a local linear fit and weight observations by the
distance between their empirical CDF value and \(\theta\), with a manual
bandwidth on the probability scale (they use \(h = 0.05\); the example
uses \(h = 0.1\)):

```{r simzhou}
fit_sz <- suppressWarnings(
  qqr(y ~ x + w, data = dat, qvar = "x", taus = taus,
      thetas = fit$thetas, kernel_space = "cdf", degree = 1, h = 0.1)
)
round(fit_sz$qcoef, 2)
```

## References

Sim, N. and Zhou, H. (2015) Oil prices, US stock return, and the dependence
between their quantiles. *Journal of Banking & Finance*, 55, 1--8.
doi:10.1016/j.jbankfin.2015.01.013
